title: Cascade Medical Supplies: allowance for doubtful accounts, percent of sales vs. aging of receivables
participant_role: Credit and collections accountant at Cascade Medical Supplies preparing the year-end bad debt adjustment
judge_role: Managing partner and treasurer of Cascade Medical Supplies, who must approve the year-end adjusting entries

difficulty.rationale: Aging vs percent of sales and the allowance adjustment.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of credit and collections accountant for CASCADE MEDICAL SUPPLIES, a wholesale distributor of diagnostic equipment, surgical disposables and clinic supplies. The managing partner and treasurer (judge) has asked you to finalize the year-end adjusting entry for uncollectible accounts.

Cascade sells on credit to regional outpatient clinics and physical therapy practices. At December 31, before adjustments, gross accounts receivable total $500,000 and the Allowance for Doubtful Accounts has a $2,000 credit balance. Net credit sales for the year were $2,000,000.

Management is considering two methods for estimating uncollectible accounts. Historical data shows that 1.5% of net credit sales become uncollectible. Management has also sorted the $500,000 of receivables by age and estimated the percentage of each group that will not be collected.

[Cascade year-end receivables data and aging schedule: see exhibits]

The treasurer (judge) wants to use the aging of receivables for the year-end entry but wants to see how both methods compare and why the company cannot simply write off accounts when customers fail to pay.

You must:
- Compute the bad debt expense and the ending allowance under both the percent of sales method and the aging of receivables method
- Prepare the year-end adjusting journal entry under the aging of receivables method
- Show how accounts receivable will be presented on the year-end balance sheet
- Explain why GAAP requires the allowance method rather than the direct write-off method

You will present the information to the treasurer (judge) in a role-play to take place in the treasurer's (judge's) office. The treasurer (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the treasurer's (judge's) questions, the treasurer (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Compute the bad debt expense and the ending allowance under both the percent of sales method and the aging of receivables method
Prepare the year-end adjusting journal entry under the aging of receivables method

judge_questions: If a clinic that owes us $1,500 goes out of business next month and we write off its account, how will that affect our net income and total assets?
What internal credit controls should Cascade put in place to reduce the $50,000 of receivables that are more than 60 days past due?

solution.overview: A strong answer computes $30,000 of expense (ending allowance $32,000) under percent of sales and a $19,000 target allowance under aging, which requires a $17,000 adjusting entry. The presenter shows net receivables of $481,000 and explains that the allowance method matches bad debts to the sales that caused them and reports receivables at the amount expected to be collected.

answer: Percent of sales (income statement approach): 2,000,000 x 1.5% = $30,000 expense; ending allowance 2,000 + 30,000 = $32,000
Aging (balance sheet approach) finds the target ending allowance: 3,000 + 6,000 + 10,000 = $19,000
Aging adjustment: 19,000 target minus 2,000 already in the allowance = $17,000 expense
Percent of sales ignores the existing balance; aging adjusts to a target balance
Debit Bad Debt Expense $17,000
Credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $17,000
The allowance now has the $19,000 credit balance the aging supports
Current assets: Accounts receivable $500,000
Less allowance for doubtful accounts ($19,000)
Net accounts receivable (net realizable value) $481,000
Matching: bad debt expense is recorded in the same year as the credit sales that caused it
Receivables are reported at the amount we actually expect to collect, not overstated
Direct write-off records the loss later, often in a different year, so it is allowed only when bad debts are immaterial
The allowance method is required for companies like Cascade with material credit sales

journal_entries.description: Dec. 31 adjusting entry for bad debts (aging method)
Next month: write off the $1,500 account of a failed clinic (judge question 1)

calculations.label: Effect of the $1,500 write-off next month
calculations.result: No effect on net income or total assets

judge_question_answers.question: If a clinic that owes us $1,500 goes out of business next month and we write off its account, how will that affect our net income and total assets?
answer: Entry: debit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $1,500, credit Accounts Receivable $1,500
Net income is not affected; the expense was already recorded in this year's estimate
Total assets do not change: gross receivables and the allowance both drop $1,500, so net receivables stay at $481,000

judge_question_answers.question: What internal credit controls should Cascade put in place to reduce the $50,000 of receivables that are more than 60 days past due?
answer: Run credit checks and set credit limits before approving orders
Put accounts on credit hold once they pass a set number of days overdue
Separate duties: the person who approves credit should not record cash receipts or write-offs
Review the aging schedule every month and follow up on past-due clinics quickly; consider early payment discounts

key_concepts.definition: Estimating uncollectible accounts at year end and recording the expense in the same period as the sales. Required under GAAP when bad debts are material.
A contra asset account that reduces accounts receivable to the amount expected to be collected.
Income statement approach: bad debt expense = net credit sales x historical loss rate, ignoring the existing allowance balance.
Balance sheet approach: receivables are grouped by age, each group is multiplied by its loss rate, and the total is the target allowance.
Adjustment = target allowance minus existing credit balance (or plus an existing debit balance).
Accounts receivable minus the allowance for doubtful accounts: the cash the company expects to collect.
Recording bad debt expense only when a specific account is written off. Allowed only when bad debts are immaterial because it breaks matching.
Debit Allowance, credit Accounts Receivable. It does not change net income or net receivables.
Expenses are recorded in the same period as the revenues they helped earn.
Policies such as credit approval, credit limits and separation of duties that protect receivables and keep records accurate.

notes: State level because students must run both estimation methods and understand why the aging adjustment subtracts the existing allowance. Watch for students who record $19,000 instead of $17,000, or who say the write-off next month reduces net income.

items.label: Explain the nature of accounts receivable

criteria.exceeds: Explains that receivables must be reported at net realizable value (the amount expected to be collected), that the allowance method matches bad debt expense to the year of the credit sales, and that direct write-off is allowed only when bad debts are immaterial, which is not the case for Cascade.
criteria.meets: Explains that GAAP requires the allowance method so bad debts are matched to the sales that caused them and receivables are not overstated.
criteria.below: Says the allowance method is required but cannot explain matching or net realizable value, or says direct write-off is never allowed under any circumstances.
criteria.little: Does not explain why the allowance method is needed, or agrees that Cascade can simply write off accounts when customers fail to pay.

criteria.exceeds: Computes both methods clearly: percent of sales gives $30,000 of expense and a $32,000 allowance; aging gives a $19,000 target ($3,000 + $6,000 + $10,000) and a $17,000 adjustment, and explains that percent of sales ignores the existing $2,000 balance while aging adjusts to a target balance.
criteria.meets: Calculates $30,000 of expense under percent of sales and the $19,000 aging target that requires a $17,000 adjustment.
criteria.below: Gets only part of the calculation, for example computes the $19,000 aging target but records it as the expense without subtracting the $2,000 existing balance.
criteria.little: Does not calculate either method, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibits.

criteria.exceeds: Records debit Bad Debt Expense $17,000, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $17,000, and explains that posting it brings the allowance to the $19,000 credit balance the aging supports.
criteria.meets: Records debit Bad Debt Expense $17,000 and credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $17,000.
criteria.below: Uses the right accounts with the wrong amount (such as $19,000 or $30,000), or reverses the debit and credit.
criteria.little: Gives no journal entry, or credits Accounts Receivable directly.

criteria.exceeds: Shows the balance sheet presentation (accounts receivable $500,000 less allowance $19,000 equals net receivables $481,000), compares it with the $468,000 that percent of sales would give, and explains that a later write-off leaves net receivables unchanged.
criteria.meets: Presents accounts receivable of $500,000 less the $19,000 allowance for net receivables of $481,000.
criteria.below: Shows the presentation with a wrong allowance or net figure, or lists only gross receivables.
criteria.little: Does not show how receivables will be presented on the balance sheet.

items.label: Explain the purpose of internal accounting controls

criteria.exceeds: Explains that controls protect assets and keep records reliable, and recommends specific credit controls for the $50,000 over 60 days past due: credit checks and limits, credit holds, separating credit approval from cash receipts and write-offs, and a monthly aging review.
criteria.meets: Recommends several credit controls, including credit checks or limits and separation of duties, and ties them to reducing past-due receivables.
criteria.below: Mentions controls in general terms, such as collecting faster, without specific practices or separation of duties.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Explains why the aging method subtracts the existing $2,000 balance and how the estimate flows into expense, the allowance and net receivables.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the $17,000 adjustment.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or misses how one step affects the next.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Supports the treasurer's choice of the aging method with a clear reason (it targets the balance expected to be uncollectible) and adds practical steps to reduce past-due accounts.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to book the $17,000 aging entry.
criteria.below: Hesitates between methods or gives a recommendation that is not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Explains both methods and the allowance in plain language the treasurer can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the calculations, entry, balance sheet and reasoning clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side table of the two methods ($30,000 vs. $17,000 expense, $32,000 vs. $19,000 allowance) or a simple T account for the allowance that makes the adjustment obvious.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the two methods easy to compare.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: the $1,500 write-off (debit Allowance, credit Accounts Receivable) does not affect net income or total assets because net receivables stay at $481,000; and names specific credit controls such as credit checks, credit holds, separation of duties and a monthly aging review.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the write-off does not reduce net income and giving at least two credit controls.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without the entry or specific controls.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says the $1,500 write-off reduces net income.

key_points: Percent of sales: $2,000,000 x 1.5% = $30,000 expense; ending allowance $32,000
Aging adjustment: $19,000 minus the existing $2,000 credit = $17,000 bad debt expense
Entry: debit Bad Debt Expense $17,000, credit Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $17,000
Balance sheet: accounts receivable $500,000 less allowance $19,000 = net receivables $481,000
GAAP requires the allowance method because it matches bad debts to the sales that caused them and reports receivables at the amount expected to be collected
Writing off the $1,500 account next month (debit Allowance, credit Accounts Receivable) does not change net income or total assets
